fixes.explanation: Yes, they cry out to the LORD, and the text says why: Jabin had nine hundred chariots of iron, and he had harshly oppressed them for twenty years (Judges 4:3). Jabin is the king of Canaan, by the way. Twenty years of that, and crying out sounds about right to me.

Right on the money. The LORD says, “And I will draw out Sisera the commander of Jabin’s army, his chariots, and his troops to the River Kishon, and I will deliver him into your hand.” (Judges 4:7) Notice who is doing the delivering. The LORD is the One who draws Sisera out and the One who delivers him.

That's what he asks. Sisera says, “Stand at the entrance to the tent, and if anyone comes and asks you, ‘Is there a man here?’ say, ‘No.’” (Judges 4:20) He is the army commander, and I bet he wants to stay hidden. So he's asking Jael to answer no if someone asks whether a man is there.

Hazor is where Jabin reigns, but Sisera doesn't mention it here. He tells Jael, “…if anyone comes and asks you, ‘Is there a man here?’ say, ‘No.’…” (Judges 4:20) He wants her to answer no to that question. He isn't asking her to point anyone anywhere.

That's what she says. Jael tells Barak, “Come, and I will show you the man you are seeking.” (Judges 4:22) Then he goes in, and Sisera lies dead with a tent peg through his temple. I think this part is heavy, so I'll just point back to what Deborah told Barak: the LORD would be selling Sisera into the hand of a woman (Judges 4:9).

Sisera had asked her to say “No” if anyone asked, “Is there a man here?” (Judges 4:20), but she doesn't say that to Barak. She tells him, “Come, and I will show you the man you are seeking.” (Judges 4:22) Then she leads Barak inside to Sisera. This part is heavy, and the text tells it plainly.

Those aren't in these verses. Here the earth trembles, the heavens pour out rain, and the clouds pour down water (Judges 5:4). The mountains quake before the LORD, the God of Israel (Judges 5:5). Drying rivers and a sun standing still aren't mentioned.

These verses don't say that. They say the earth trembled, the heavens poured out rain and the clouds poured down water (Judges 5:4). Then the mountains quaked before the LORD (Judges 5:5). Nothing about the sea or the wind shows up there.

Nobody's out house hunting in that verse. The song says, “When they chose new gods, then war came to their gates.” (Judges 5:8) What they chose was gods, and the song puts war right after it. I think that's a line worth sitting with.

Not Sisera. At the watering places, the singers “…recount the righteous acts of the LORD, the righteous deeds of His villagers in Israel.” (Judges 5:11) Sisera is the commander of Jabin's army. What they recount there is the LORD's righteous acts.

The song says Zebulun and Naphtali risked their lives (Judges 5:18), but that's not what it says about Reuben. For Reuben it says, “In the clans of Reuben there was great indecision.” (Judges 5:15) It repeats the line in the next verse. Reuben is one of Israel's tribes.

That's her. “Sisera’s mother looked through the window; she peered through the lattice and lamented: ‘Why is his chariot so long in coming?’” (Judges 5:28) Sisera is Jabin's army commander. I think this moment is heavy, so I'll let the song's words stand.

That's not who the song names. Saul was the man the LORD chose (1 Samuel 10:24), and he doesn't appear in this song. It's “Sisera’s mother” at the window, asking why his chariot is so long in coming (Judges 5:28). Sisera is Jabin's army commander.

Yes. She keeps telling herself, “Are they not finding and dividing the spoil…” (Judges 5:30) That's what she keeps telling herself, right after her wisest ladies answer. This part is heavy, and the song lets it speak for itself.
